stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure woke up unable to breathe. He is sitting bolt upright, alert, and following commands. RR 30 and labored, crackles in both lungs, SpO2 86% on room air, BP 168/96, HR 112. What is the best intervention?
opts: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula at 2 L/min and transport him sitting up
Lay him supine on the stretcher and apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Apply CPAP per protocol and coach him to tolerate the mask
Begin bag-valve-mask ventilations at 1 breath every 6 seconds with oxygen
key: An alert, cooperative patient with pulmonary edema, respiratory distress, and adequate BP is a CPAP candidate.
why: He is in respiratory distress with hypoxia and signs of pulmonary edema, yet he is alert, protecting his airway, and normotensive. CPAP recruits fluid-filled alveoli and reduces work of breathing, often avoiding the need for assisted ventilation.
wrong: Low-flow cannula oxygen is inadequate for severe hypoxia and distress from pulmonary edema.
Lying flat worsens dyspnea from pulmonary edema, and a nonrebreather gives no positive pressure.
He is breathing spontaneously at an adequate rate with intact mental status; BVM ventilation is for inadequate breathing.

stem: You are deciding whether CPAP is appropriate for a 74-year-old woman with severe shortness of breath. Which TWO of the following findings, if present, would be contraindications to CPAP? Select TWO.
opts: She opens her eyes only to painful stimuli
Her blood pressure is 80/52 mm Hg
She has COPD and audible expiratory wheezing
Her respiratory rate is 28 with accessory muscle use
Her SpO2 is 88% despite a nonrebreather mask
key: CPAP requires a patient who is alert enough to protect the airway and has adequate blood pressure.
why: CPAP needs a conscious patient who can follow commands and protect the airway; a patient responding only to pain needs assisted ventilation instead. Positive pressure reduces venous return, so hypotension is a contraindication.
wrong: A COPD exacerbation with distress in an alert patient is a common CPAP indication.
Tachypnea with accessory muscle use is the distress CPAP is meant to treat.
Persistent hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen supports the use of CPAP rather than ruling it out.

stem: Ten minutes after you start CPAP on a 61-year-old man with COPD, he becomes difficult to arouse. His respirations drop to 8/min and shallow, and SpO2 falls from 90% to 82%. What should you do next?
opts: Remove CPAP and ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
Increase the CPAP pressure setting to improve his oxygenation
Replace CPAP with a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Continue CPAP and recheck his mental status in 5 minutes
key: Falling mental status or hypoventilation on CPAP means CPAP has failed; switch to assisted ventilation.
why: CPAP only supports a patient who is breathing adequately on his own. Decreasing responsiveness with a slow, shallow rate is respiratory failure, so the EMT removes CPAP and provides BVM ventilation with oxygen.
wrong: More pressure does not fix hypoventilation; CPAP depends on adequate spontaneous breathing.
A nonrebreather cannot help a patient who is not moving enough air; he needs assisted ventilation.
Waiting lets hypoventilation progress toward arrest; he needs ventilation now.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with COPD is in severe respiratory distress. She is alert, leaning forward with her hands on her knees, and resists lying back. You have applied oxygen. How should you position her for transport?
opts: Supine on the stretcher with her legs elevated about 12 inches
Left lateral recumbent with her knees drawn up toward her chest
Supine and secured flat to keep her from moving during transport
Sitting upright on the stretcher in her position of comfort
key: An alert patient in respiratory distress is transported sitting upright in a position of comfort.
why: Sitting upright lets the diaphragm descend and the accessory muscles work, reducing the work of breathing. An alert patient who chooses a tripod position is telling you how she breathes best.
wrong: Lying flat with the legs raised increases work of breathing and is not a treatment for dyspnea.
The lateral position is for patients who cannot protect their own airway; she is alert and needs upright positioning.
There is no trauma indication, and lying flat worsens her dyspnea.

stem: A 50-year-old man is found unresponsive on a couch after heavy drinking. There is no sign of trauma. He is breathing 16/min with good chest rise, SpO2 95%, and he has vomited. After you suction his mouth, how should you position him?
opts: Supine, with your partner holding a head-tilt chin-lift
Supine with the foot of the stretcher raised above his head
Semi-sitting at 45 degrees with his head supported by a pillow
On his side in the recovery position, with suction ready
key: An unresponsive, adequately breathing patient without suspected spinal injury goes in the recovery position.
why: He is breathing adequately but cannot protect his airway and has already vomited. The lateral recovery position lets fluid drain from the mouth and reduces aspiration risk while you keep suction ready.
wrong: Supine positioning leaves him at high risk of aspirating more vomit, even with a manual maneuver.
Head-down positioning increases aspiration risk and has no benefit here.
Semi-sitting lets his head fall forward or back and does not drain the airway.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had crushing substernal chest pain for 20 minutes. He is alert, has no allergies, takes no blood thinners, and denies recent bleeding. BP 150/88, HR 96, SpO2 97%. Your protocol includes aspirin for suspected acute coronary syndrome. What should you do?
opts: Apply a nonrebreather mask and leave aspirin for the emergency department
Have him swallow an adult aspirin whole with a full glass of water
Give chewable aspirin per protocol and have him chew it
Withhold aspirin until a 12-lead ECG confirms a heart attack
key: Suspected ACS without contraindications: give chewable aspirin per protocol; do not wait for diagnostic confirmation.
why: Aspirin reduces platelet aggregation and lowers mortality in ACS, and chewing speeds absorption. He has no allergy or bleeding history, so it should be given promptly on clinical suspicion.
wrong: His SpO2 is normal so high-flow oxygen is not indicated, and delaying aspirin loses its benefit.
Aspirin for ACS is chewed for faster absorption; swallowing it whole with a large volume of water is not the method.
Aspirin is given on clinical suspicion of ACS and should not wait for ECG confirmation.

stem: A 64-year-old woman has chest pressure radiating to her jaw. You are preparing to give aspirin per protocol. Which findings would make you withhold aspirin? Select TWO.
opts: Hives and throat swelling the last time she took aspirin
Black, tarry stools over the past two days
She took her daily low-dose aspirin this morning
She is 64 years old and has diabetes
She is nauseated and sweating
key: Aspirin is withheld for known aspirin allergy and for signs of active bleeding such as GI bleeding.
why: A prior allergic reaction to aspirin could recur as anaphylaxis. Black, tarry stools suggest an active upper GI bleed, which aspirin's antiplatelet effect would worsen.
wrong: A daily low-dose aspirin is not a contraindication; follow protocol for the ACS dose.
Age and diabetes raise ACS risk; they are not reasons to withhold aspirin.
Nausea and diaphoresis are typical ACS findings, not contraindications.

stem: A 62-year-old man with prescribed nitroglycerin has chest pain. BP 138/84, HR 88. During your history he mentions he took tadalafil for erectile dysfunction last night. He asks you to help him take a nitroglycerin tablet. What is the best action?
opts: Assist with one tablet, since his blood pressure is adequate
Lay him supine first, then assist him with one tablet
Assist with half a tablet to reduce the chance of a drug interaction
Withhold nitroglycerin and notify medical direction of the tadalafil use
key: Recent PDE-5 inhibitor use contraindicates nitroglycerin, regardless of the current blood pressure.
why: Combining nitrates with a PDE-5 inhibitor can cause severe, prolonged hypotension; nitrates are avoided within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil and within 48 hours of tadalafil. The EMT withholds nitroglycerin, reports the drug use, and continues other chest pain care such as aspirin if not contraindicated.
wrong: A normal BP now does not protect against the profound hypotension caused by the interaction.
Positioning does not make the combination safe; the drug should not be given.
EMTs do not alter the prescribed dose, and any nitrate is contraindicated after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.

stem: Each patient below has chest pain and asks for help with nitroglycerin. Classify whether the EMT should assist (with protocol or medical direction) or withhold it.
rows: Alert, BP 146/90, own unexpired prescription, no PDE-5 inhibitor use
Pale and clammy with BP below the protocol minimum
The tablets are prescribed to the patient's spouse
Pain persists after one dose, BP still 150/92, protocol allows a repeat dose
key: Assist only with the patient's own nitroglycerin when BP is adequate and there is no PDE-5 inhibitor use.
why: The rights of medication administration require the right patient and right drug, so a spouse's prescription is not used. Hypotension and recent PDE-5 inhibitor use are contraindications, while a repeat dose with adequate BP follows protocol.

stem: A 24-year-old woman was stung by a wasp 10 minutes ago. She has hives across her trunk, a hoarse voice, wheezing, and BP 84/50. She carries her own prescribed epinephrine auto-injector. What should you do first?
opts: Apply a cold pack to the sting site and reassess her in 5 minutes
Give high-flow oxygen and reassess before deciding on epinephrine
Have her take the diphenhydramine tablets she carries in her purse
Administer her epinephrine auto-injector into the lateral thigh
key: Anaphylaxis with airway or circulatory involvement is treated first with the patient's epinephrine auto-injector.
why: Hoarseness, wheezing, and hypotension after a sting indicate anaphylaxis. Epinephrine reverses airway swelling, bronchospasm, and vasodilation, and any delay worsens outcomes; the lateral thigh is the injection site.
wrong: A cold pack does nothing for airway swelling or shock from anaphylaxis.
Oxygen is supportive, but delaying epinephrine in anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory signs is harmful.
Oral antihistamines act slowly, are not an EMT treatment, and do not reverse airway swelling or shock.

stem: Four minutes ago you gave a 30-year-old man his epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis. His wheezing has eased and BP rose from 82/50 to 108/70. He now feels shaky and anxious, and his heart rate is 124. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Explain that tremor is an expected effect, keep reassessing, and transport
Give a second auto-injector now because his heart rate is elevated
Stop oxygen and allow him to refuse transport since he has improved
Apply a constricting band above the injection site to slow absorption
key: After epinephrine, reassess and transport; tachycardia and tremor are expected effects, and symptoms can return.
why: Shakiness, anxiety, and tachycardia are common epinephrine side effects and show the drug is working. Anaphylaxis can recur as the drug wears off, so the EMT reassesses vital signs and breathing, documents the time given, and transports.
wrong: Tachycardia is an expected side effect, not an indication for another dose; repeat dosing is for persistent or returning anaphylaxis per protocol.
Symptoms can return as epinephrine wears off, so he needs transport and ongoing reassessment.
Restricting absorption would blunt the drug's effect and is not done.

stem: Medical direction approves assisting a 19-year-old with asthma, who is alert and can follow instructions, with her prescribed albuterol metered-dose inhaler. Place the steps in the correct order.
opts: Confirm the inhaler is prescribed to her, is the right drug, and is not expired
Shake the inhaler
Have her exhale fully
Have her seal her lips on the mouthpiece and inhale deeply as the canister is pressed
Have her hold her breath as long as comfortable, then exhale
Reassess her breathing, SpO2, and vital signs and document the dose
key: Assisting with an MDI: verify the rights, shake, exhale, inhale with actuation, hold breath, then reassess.
why: Verifying right patient, drug, and expiration comes before any administration. A full exhalation followed by a deep inhalation during actuation and a breath hold delivers the drug to the lungs, and reassessment shows whether it worked.

stem: A 16-year-old with asthma has used his albuterol inhaler repeatedly at home without relief. He is now drowsy and speaks one word at a time. RR 8 and shallow, SpO2 84%, with very little wheezing heard. His mother hands you the inhaler. What is the best action?
opts: Assist him with two puffs of his albuterol, then reassess
Apply CPAP and coach him to slow his breathing
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and let him rest
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen and request ALS
key: A drowsy asthmatic with slow, shallow breaths and a quiet chest needs assisted ventilation, not an inhaler.
why: Altered mental status, a falling respiratory rate, and diminished wheezing signal impending respiratory arrest. He cannot take the deep, coordinated breath an MDI needs, so the priority is BVM ventilation with oxygen and ALS support.
wrong: He cannot generate an effective inhalation, and failing ventilation must be supported first.
CPAP requires an alert patient breathing adequately on his own; he is hypoventilating with altered mental status.
A nonrebreather cannot help a patient who is not moving enough air.

stem: A 47-year-old man with diabetes is confused and sweaty after skipping lunch. He answers slowly but is awake, follows commands, and swallows without difficulty. His glucose reads 42 mg/dL. What should you do?
opts: Withhold treatment and request ALS for intravenous dextrose
Give nothing by mouth and transport him in the recovery position
Help him take a dose of his own prescribed insulin
Give oral glucose per protocol and reassess his mental status
key: Oral glucose is for a hypoglycemic patient who is awake enough to swallow and protect the airway.
why: He has symptomatic hypoglycemia, a history of diabetes, and an intact gag and swallow. Oral glucose is within EMT scope and works quickly; reassessing mental status shows whether it is effective.
wrong: He meets criteria for oral glucose now, and waiting delays treatment of symptomatic hypoglycemia.
He can swallow and protect his airway, so withholding oral glucose is unnecessary.
Insulin lowers blood glucose further and is not an EMT medication.

stem: A 30-year-old man is found unresponsive with a syringe nearby. He has a carotid pulse of 60, respirations 4/min and shallow, cyanotic lips, and pinpoint pupils. Your partner is preparing intranasal naloxone. What should you do first?
opts: Hold airway care until naloxone has had time to take effect
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and monitor
Begin chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute
Open the airway and ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
key: In opioid overdose with a pulse and inadequate breathing, ventilate first; naloxone is given in addition.
why: His immediate threat is hypoxia from respiratory depression. Bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen corrects it right away, while naloxone takes minutes to work and is given alongside ventilation, not instead of it.
wrong: Waiting for naloxone leaves him hypoxic for minutes; ventilation must not be delayed.
A nonrebreather cannot help a patient breathing 4 shallow breaths per minute.
He has a pulse, so compressions are not indicated; he needs ventilation.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with epilepsy has had one generalized seizure after another for 8 minutes without regaining consciousness. She is still seizing and has cyanosis around her lips. What is the best management?
opts: Place a bite block between her teeth and hold her arms still to prevent injury
Wait for the seizure activity to stop on its own before beginning any care
Protect her from injury, suction and give oxygen, request ALS, and transport promptly
Give oral glucose between her cheek and gum in case her blood sugar is low
key: Continuous or back-to-back seizures without recovery are status epilepticus: protect, support airway, get ALS, transport.
why: Seizures lasting more than about 5 minutes or recurring without return of consciousness are status epilepticus, which causes hypoxia and brain injury. The EMT prevents injury, maintains the airway with suction and oxygen, and gets her to ALS and definitive care quickly.
wrong: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or obstruct the airway, and restraining limbs can cause injury.
Status epilepticus is an emergency; waiting allows hypoxia and brain injury to progress.
Nothing should be put in the mouth of a seizing patient; she cannot swallow safely.

stem: A 66-year-old man's wife says he was fine at breakfast 45 minutes ago, then suddenly could not lift his right arm and his speech became slurred. He is alert. BP 178/100, HR 84, SpO2 97%. What is the most important information to obtain and report?
opts: The exact time he was last known to be well
A complete list of every surgery he has had
Whether his symptoms improve after a dose of aspirin
A series of blood pressures taken on scene before moving him
key: In suspected stroke, the last-known-well time determines treatment options and must be obtained and reported.
why: Clot-dissolving and clot-removal treatments are time-limited, and eligibility is based on when the patient was last known to be normal. Getting this time accurately from a witness and reporting it early lets the hospital prepare.
wrong: A full surgical history is lower priority than time-critical stroke information and should not delay transport.
Aspirin is not given for suspected stroke in the field because a hemorrhagic stroke cannot be ruled out.
Extra scene time delays treatment; vital signs are repeated en route.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with diabetes is found by her daughter in bed. She moans only to painful stimulus, with snoring respirations at 14/min and SpO2 93%. Her glucose reads 31 mg/dL. The daughter hands you a tube of oral glucose. What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Squeeze the full tube of oral glucose between her cheek and gum now
Have the daughter give her small sips of orange juice while you transport
Open the airway, give oxygen, request ALS, and do not give oral glucose
Leave her supine as found and recheck her glucose level in 10 minutes
key: Oral glucose is withheld from a patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway; manage the airway and get ALS.
why: She responds only to pain and has snoring respirations, so she cannot protect her airway and could aspirate anything given by mouth. The EMT opens and maintains the airway, gives oxygen, and requests ALS for intravenous dextrose.
wrong: She cannot swallow or protect her airway, so oral glucose could be aspirated.
Any oral fluid risks aspiration in a patient without an adequate gag and swallow.
She will not improve without treatment, and her snoring airway needs to be opened now.

stem: A 27-year-old man is found unresponsive at a party. Bystanders say he took some pills. Which findings would most strongly support an opioid toxidrome? Select THREE.
opts: Pupils constricted to pinpoint size
Respiratory rate of 6 with shallow breaths
Depressed level of consciousness
Hot, dry, flushed skin
Widely dilated pupils
Agitation with a heart rate of 140
key: The opioid toxidrome is depressed consciousness, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils.
why: Opioids depress the brainstem respiratory drive and level of consciousness and constrict the pupils. Recognizing the pattern points the EMT to ventilation and naloxone.
wrong: Hot, dry, flushed skin suggests an anticholinergic agent.
Dilated pupils point toward stimulants or anticholinergic agents.
Agitation with marked tachycardia suggests a sympathomimetic agent.

stem: Your agency is reviewing poisoning calls from the past month. Classify each set of findings by the toxidrome it most likely represents.
rows: Agitated, dilated pupils, sweating, HR 150, BP 190/110
Farmworker with drooling, tearing, wheezing, vomiting, small pupils
Confused, hot dry red skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention
key: Toxidromes are recognized by pattern: pupils, skin, mental status, vital signs, and secretions.
why: Opioids cause sedation, small pupils, and slow breathing. Stimulants cause agitation, sweating, tachycardia, and hypertension; organophosphate (cholinergic) poisoning causes excess secretions and bronchorrhea; anticholinergics cause dry, hot skin, dilated pupils, confusion, and urinary retention.

stem: Police ask you to transport a combative 32-year-old man who is a danger to himself. Medical direction approves physical restraint per protocol. Which restraint position is safest?
opts: Prone, with his wrists and ankles tied together behind him
Seated upright, with a blanket wrapped tightly around his chest
Prone, with an officer kneeling on his back until he is calm
Supine or on his side, limbs secured, with continuous airway monitoring
key: Restrained patients are kept supine or on the side, never prone or hobbled, with continuous monitoring.
why: Prone and hobbled positions and pressure on the back restrict chest movement and are linked to positional asphyxia and sudden death. Supine or lateral restraint lets the EMT watch the airway and breathing throughout transport.
wrong: Prone hog-tie positioning is associated with positional asphyxia and sudden death.
A tightly wrapped chest restricts breathing.
Weight on the back restricts chest expansion and can cause asphyxia.

stem: A 28-year-old man is restrained on your stretcher for severe agitation. He has been shouting and struggling, is sweating, and is hot to the touch. Halfway to the hospital he suddenly becomes quiet and still. What should you do immediately?
opts: Check his responsiveness, breathing, and pulse
Note the time he calmed down and recheck vitals on arrival
Loosen one restraint to reward him for calming down
Place a spit hood over his face to prevent more shouting
key: A sudden calm in an agitated, restrained patient may be respiratory or cardiac arrest; assess at once.
why: Severely agitated, hyperthermic patients who struggle against restraint are at risk of sudden cardiac arrest. Abrupt quiet is a warning sign, so the EMT immediately checks responsiveness, breathing, and pulse and is ready to start CPR.
wrong: Waiting until arrival could miss an arrest that needs immediate CPR.
Loosening a restraint does not address possible arrest and may create a safety risk.
A spit hood does not address sudden collapse and can hide airway problems.

stem: An 81-year-old nursing home resident has new confusion and two days of painful urination. Temperature 101.8°F, HR 118, RR 26, BP 88/54, SpO2 93%. Which actions are most appropriate? Select TWO.
opts: Apply oxygen and closely monitor her mental status and vital signs for worsening shock
Notify the receiving hospital early that you suspect sepsis
Stay on scene to complete a detailed head-to-toe exam first
Give her oral fluids to treat dehydration before leaving
Treat the confusion as her baseline dementia and transport non-emergently
key: Suspected sepsis with hypotension: support oxygenation and perfusion, transport promptly, and pre-notify the hospital.
why: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and new confusion with a likely urinary source suggest septic shock. The EMT supports oxygenation (SpO2 93%), watches for deterioration, transports promptly, and pre-notifies the hospital so antibiotics and fluids can start quickly.
wrong: Prolonged scene time delays definitive treatment for septic shock.
A confused patient should not be given oral fluids because of aspiration risk.
New confusion with fever and hypotension is an emergency and should not be assumed to be baseline.

stem: A 25-year-old man was stabbed in the right chest. You hear air moving through the wound with each breath and see bubbling blood. He is alert, RR 28, SpO2 91%. After covering the wound with your gloved hand, what is the best next step?
opts: Pack the wound tightly with hemostatic gauze
Decompress the chest with a needle in the second intercostal space
Cover the wound with a loosely taped dry gauze pad
Apply a vented chest seal or occlusive dressing per protocol
key: An open (sucking) chest wound is sealed with a vented chest seal or occlusive dressing per protocol.
why: An occlusive seal stops air from entering the pleural space through the wound. A vented seal lets air escape on exhalation, which lowers the risk of tension pneumothorax.
wrong: Wound packing is for extremity and junctional bleeding, and it does not seal an open chest wound.
Needle decompression is outside EMT scope.
Gauze alone lets air keep entering the chest.

stem: You sealed a gunshot wound to a man's left chest with a non-vented occlusive dressing. Ten minutes later he is anxious, RR 36, SpO2 84%, BP 80/50, with distended neck veins and absent breath sounds on the left. What should you do?
opts: Apply a second occlusive dressing over the first one to make the seal more airtight
Lay him flat and elevate his legs about 12 inches to treat the hypotension
Briefly lift a corner of the dressing to release trapped air, then reseal and expedite ALS
Increase the oxygen flow rate, leave the dressing in place, and reassess in 5 minutes
key: Signs of tension pneumothorax after sealing a chest wound: briefly unseal (burp) the dressing and expedite ALS.
why: Worsening distress, hypotension, distended neck veins, and absent breath sounds after a seal suggest air trapped under pressure. Lifting the dressing edge may let air escape, and the patient needs rapid transport and ALS for decompression.
wrong: More sealing traps more air and worsens tension physiology.
Leg elevation does not relieve the pressure collapsing his lung and impeding venous return.
Waiting allows tension pneumothorax to progress to cardiac arrest.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has a knife wound to the abdomen with a loop of intestine protruding. She is alert, BP 112/70, HR 104. What is the correct wound care?
opts: Gently push the intestine back inside and tape a dressing over the wound
Cover the organs with dry sterile gauze and place an ice pack on top
Apply a firm pressure dressing directly over the exposed intestine
Cover with a moist sterile dressing and an occlusive layer, and keep her warm
key: An evisceration is covered with a moist sterile dressing and an occlusive layer; organs are never replaced.
why: Moist sterile dressings keep exposed bowel from drying, and an occlusive covering limits heat and moisture loss. Pushing organs back in risks contamination and injury.
wrong: Replacing organs risks infection and further injury.
Dry gauze sticks to tissue, and cold promotes heat loss.
Pressure on exposed bowel can damage it and reduce its blood flow.

stem: A construction worker has a 10-inch piece of rebar impaled in his left thigh. Bleeding around it is minimal, and he is alert with normal vital signs. Transport will take 15 minutes. How should you manage the object?
opts: Remove it slowly and then apply direct pressure to the wound
Have it cut flush with the skin so it fits on the stretcher
Stabilize it in place with bulky dressings and secure it
Pull it out partway to judge how deep it goes
key: Impaled objects are stabilized in place unless they obstruct the airway or prevent CPR.
why: The object may be tamponading damaged vessels, so removing or moving it can cause severe bleeding. Bulky dressings around it limit movement during transport.
wrong: Removal can unleash uncontrolled bleeding; impaled objects stay in place.
Cutting it flush removes your ability to stabilize it and may move it deeper.
Any movement can worsen tissue injury and bleeding.

stem: A 30-year-old motorcyclist with a head injury responds only to pain. Breathing is irregular at 6/min. Pupils are equal and reactive, with no posturing. BP 126/80, SpO2 88%. You begin BVM ventilation with oxygen. At what rate should you ventilate?
opts: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds to blow off carbon dioxide
One breath every 12 seconds to limit gastric distension
One breath every 6 seconds, avoiding hyperventilation
As fast as possible until his SpO2 reaches 100%
key: Ventilate head-injured adults at a normal rate (about 1 breath every 6 s); avoid routine hyperventilation.
why: Both hypoxia and hyperventilation worsen secondary brain injury. Without signs of herniation, the goal is normal ventilation at about 10 breaths per minute with oxygen, which prevents hypoxia without constricting cerebral blood vessels.
wrong: Routine hyperventilation constricts cerebral vessels and reduces brain blood flow.
Five breaths per minute is too slow and allows hypoxia and carbon dioxide buildup.
Uncontrolled rapid ventilation causes hyperventilation, gastric distension, and reduced cardiac output.

stem: You are ventilating an adult with a severe head injury with a BVM at 10 breaths/min. During transport his GCS falls from 8 to 5, his right pupil becomes dilated and sluggish, and he develops extensor posturing. SpO2 97%, BP 150/70, HR 58. What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Stop assisted ventilation and switch him to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Elevate his legs to increase blood flow to the brain and recheck his pupils
Keep ventilating with oxygen and expedite transport to a trauma center with notification
Divert to the closest clinic so that a physician can evaluate him sooner
key: Signs of herniation call for continued oxygenation and ventilation, rapid transport to a trauma center, and early notification.
why: A falling GCS, a unilateral dilated pupil, posturing, and Cushing-type vital signs suggest rising intracranial pressure and possible herniation. The EMT prevents hypoxia, keeps ventilating, and gets him to neurosurgical care quickly; any change in ventilation rate for herniation is a protocol or medical-direction decision, not a routine step.
wrong: He cannot breathe adequately on his own; stopping ventilation causes hypoxia, which worsens secondary brain injury.
Leg elevation does not treat rising intracranial pressure and is not a treatment for herniation.
A clinic cannot provide neurosurgical care; diverting there delays definitive treatment.

stem: A 22-year-old man has a single gunshot wound to the left upper abdomen. He is alert and oriented, moves all extremities with normal sensation, and has no neck or back pain or tenderness. BP 94/60, HR 120. What is the best approach to spinal care?
opts: Secure him to a long backboard with a cervical collar before moving him
Apply a cervical collar, since all penetrating trauma requires one
Withhold spinal motion restriction; control bleeding and transport rapidly
Delay transport until a scoop stretcher can be brought to the scene
key: Penetrating trauma alone, without neurologic deficit or other indications, does not call for spinal motion restriction.
why: The 2018 joint statement lists altered mental status, midline tenderness, focal deficits, spinal deformity, and distracting injury as indications; penetrating trauma alone is not one. Spinal precautions here would only delay transport of a patient in shock.
wrong: He has no SMR indication, and boarding delays transport of a hypotensive patient.
Penetrating trauma alone is not an SMR indication under the joint statement.
Delaying transport for a patient with penetrating trauma and shock increases mortality.

stem: Using the 2018 joint position statement on spinal motion restriction, classify each injured patient.
rows: Fell 8 feet from a ladder, intoxicated, cannot reliably report pain
Tingling and weakness in both hands after a shallow-water dive
Midline tenderness over the lower neck after a rear-end collision
Low-speed collision; alert, sober, no midline tenderness, normal neuro exam, no distracting injury
Isolated stab wound to the flank; alert, normal motor and sensory exam
key: SMR indications: altered mental status or intoxication, midline tenderness, focal deficit, deformity, distracting injury.
why: Intoxication, focal neurologic symptoms, and midline spinal tenderness each meet SMR criteria. An alert, sober patient with a normal exam and no tenderness, and a penetrating injury without neurologic findings, do not.

stem: A 34-year-old man fell from a horse and has a painful, deformed mid-thigh. You are deciding whether to apply a traction splint to that leg. Which additional findings would contraindicate a traction splint? Select TWO.
opts: An open, deformed ankle fracture on the same leg
Suspected pelvic fracture with pelvic pain and instability
Mid-thigh deformity with shortening of the leg
Intact distal pulse, motor function, and sensation
Muscle spasm causing severe thigh pain
key: Traction splints are for isolated midshaft femur fractures; pelvic, hip, knee, or same-leg ankle injury contraindicates them.
why: The traction splint anchors at the ischium and pulls from the ankle, so a pelvic fracture or an injured ankle on the same leg would be worsened by its use. A closed, isolated midshaft femur fracture is the indication.
wrong: Midshaft femur deformity with shortening is the classic indication for traction.
Intact distal circulation and sensation are expected findings and are rechecked after splinting.
Traction relieves the muscle spasm that causes femur fracture pain.

stem: A 45-year-old man caught his hand in a table saw, amputating two fingers. Bleeding from the stumps is controlled with direct pressure. A coworker hands you the fingers. How should you care for the amputated parts?
opts: Wrap in moist sterile gauze per protocol, seal in a plastic bag, and keep it cool
Place them directly on ice in a cooler so they stay as cold as possible
Submerge them in a container of tap water to keep them from drying out
Leave them with the coworker to bring to the hospital later by car
key: Amputated parts are wrapped in sterile gauze, sealed in a bag, kept cool without direct ice, and transported with the patient.
why: Cooling slows tissue breakdown, but direct contact with ice or water damages tissue and can prevent reattachment. The part travels with the patient so the surgical team can evaluate it promptly.
wrong: Direct ice contact causes freezing injury that can prevent reattachment.
Soaking in water causes tissue swelling and damage that can prevent reattachment.
Parts should travel with the patient to avoid delay in evaluation for reattachment.

stem: A 38-year-old worker spilled dry powdered lime on both forearms. Powder is still visible on his skin and clothing. The scene is safe and you are wearing appropriate PPE. What should you do first?
opts: Brush off the powder and remove contaminated clothing, then irrigate with lots of water
Flush the powder off right away with large amounts of water before removing any clothing
Apply a vinegar solution to neutralize the chemical, then rinse the arms with water
Cover both arms with dry sterile dressings, keep him warm, and transport promptly
key: Dry chemicals are brushed off first, then the skin is irrigated with large amounts of water.
why: Some dry chemicals such as lime react with water, so the EMT brushes off as much powder as possible and removes contaminated clothing first. Copious irrigation then removes the remaining chemical.
wrong: Adding water to a large amount of dry lime can activate it; brush it off first.
Neutralizing agents can generate heat and worsen the injury.
Covering the arms leaves the chemical in contact with the skin.

stem: A 41-year-old lineman contacted a power line. The utility confirms the line is de-energized. He is alert, has a small charred wound on his right palm and another on his left foot, and says his chest feels 'fluttery.' HR 110 and irregular. What is the priority concern?
opts: Possible dysrhythmia and hidden deep tissue damage; keep the AED ready and transport
Minor injury, because small skin wounds indicate little energy passed through him
Cooling both wounds with ice packs to stop the burning process in deeper tissue
Applying burn ointment to both wounds before covering them with sterile dressings
key: Electrical injury can cause dysrhythmias and deep tissue damage far beyond the visible entry and exit wounds.
why: Current passing through the body can disrupt cardiac rhythm and damage muscle and nerves along its path. An irregular pulse and palpitations require cardiac readiness and transport, often to a burn or trauma center per protocol.
wrong: Small skin wounds greatly underestimate deep tissue damage along the current path.
Ice causes further tissue injury and can cause hypothermia.
Ointments are not applied in the field; burns are covered with dry sterile dressings.

stem: You are assisting with an uncomplicated head-first delivery of a term infant at home. Place the steps in the correct order.
opts: Support the head with gentle pressure as it delivers to prevent an explosive delivery
Check for an umbilical cord around the infant's neck
Gently guide the head downward to deliver the upper (anterior) shoulder
Guide the head upward to deliver the lower (posterior) shoulder
Support and grasp the infant as the body delivers
Dry, warm, and stimulate the newborn
key: Normal delivery: control the head, check for a nuchal cord, deliver anterior then posterior shoulder, then the body.
why: Gentle control of the head prevents tearing, and a nuchal cord must be found before the shoulders deliver. Downward then upward guidance delivers the shoulders in sequence, and drying and warming the newborn prevents heat loss.

stem: During a delivery, the infant's head has emerged, and you feel the umbilical cord wrapped tightly around the neck. You try but cannot slip it over the head. What should you do?
opts: Pull firmly on the head to complete the delivery quickly
Clamp the cord in two places, cut between the clamps, and unwrap it
Push the head back into the vagina and transport rapidly
Wait for the next contraction to loosen the cord on its own
key: A nuchal cord that cannot be slipped over the head is clamped in two places and cut between the clamps.
why: A loose cord is slipped over the head, but a tight one can compress the infant's blood supply and prevent delivery. Clamping twice and cutting between the clamps frees the infant without bleeding from either end.
wrong: Traction on the head can injure the infant and tighten the cord further.
Pushing the head back is not done for a nuchal cord and delays delivery.
Waiting lets a tight cord continue to compress blood flow.

stem: A 29-year-old in active labor says she feels something between her legs. You see a loop of pulsating umbilical cord protruding from the vagina; the baby's head is not visible. What is the best action?
opts: Push the cord gently back into the vagina, cover it with a towel, and transport
Have her push hard with the next contraction so that the baby delivers before transport
Elevate her hips, lift the presenting part off the cord with gloved fingers, and transport
Clamp the cord in two places and cut between the clamps to relieve tension
key: Prolapsed cord: relieve pressure on the cord by positioning and lifting the presenting part; transport rapidly.
why: The presenting part compresses the cord against the pelvis and cuts off fetal blood flow. Hips-elevated or knee-chest positioning and lifting the presenting part off the cord relieve the pressure; the exposed cord is kept moist and the mother is transported immediately.
wrong: Replacing the cord is not attempted; it does not relieve compression and risks injury.
Pushing drives the presenting part against the cord and worsens compression.
Cutting the cord stops all blood flow to the fetus.

stem: During a breech delivery, the infant's buttocks, legs, and body deliver, but the head has not delivered after about 3 minutes despite contractions. What should you do?
opts: Pull firmly on the infant's legs and body to deliver the head with the next push
Use gloved fingers to hold the vaginal wall off the infant's face and transport rapidly
Push the infant's body back into the birth canal and transport the mother rapidly
Keep supporting the body and wait for the head to deliver without intervening
key: If a breech head does not deliver, create an airway with gloved fingers and transport rapidly.
why: An entrapped head compresses the cord, and the infant may attempt to breathe with the face against the vaginal wall. Holding the tissue away from the mouth and nose gives an airway while the mother is rushed to the hospital.
wrong: Traction on the body can injure the infant's neck and spinal cord.
Pushing the body back is not attempted and causes injury.
Waiting allows prolonged cord compression and hypoxia.

stem: Ten minutes after delivery of the placenta, a 31-year-old woman continues to bleed heavily from the vagina. She is pale, HR 122, BP 92/58. Her lower abdomen feels soft and boggy. Besides treating for shock, what should you do?
opts: Pack the vagina tightly with sterile gauze to apply pressure to the bleeding
Massage the uterine fundus firmly and encourage breastfeeding if the infant is stable
Sit her upright on the stretcher with her legs crossed to slow the bleeding
Stay on scene and recheck her vital signs until the bleeding slows on its own
key: Postpartum hemorrhage with a boggy uterus is treated with fundal massage and breastfeeding, plus shock care and transport.
why: A soft, boggy uterus is not contracting to compress its bleeding vessels. Fundal massage and nipple stimulation from breastfeeding both promote uterine contraction while the EMT treats shock and transports.
wrong: Nothing is placed inside the vagina; pads are placed externally.
Sitting does not control bleeding and worsens hypotension.
Ongoing hemorrhage with shock requires immediate transport.

stem: A term newborn is limp and not breathing after delivery. Place the steps of care in the correct order.
opts: Warm, dry, and stimulate the newborn
Position the head to open the airway; suction only if secretions obstruct it
Assess breathing and heart rate
Begin positive-pressure ventilation if apneic, gasping, or heart rate below 100/min
Begin compressions at 3:1 if heart rate stays below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation
key: Newborn care: warm, dry, stimulate, position airway, assess, ventilate if needed, compress only if HR stays below 60.
why: Most newborns respond to warming, drying, stimulation, and an open airway. Ventilation is the most important intervention for a newborn who is apneic or bradycardic, and compressions start only if the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation.

stem: A woman who is 34 weeks pregnant was lying on her back on the floor when she became dizzy and nauseated. She is pale, HR 110, BP 88/56. There is no trauma. How should you position her?
opts: Supine with her legs elevated
On her left side
Sitting upright at 90 degrees
Prone with her head turned to one side
key: Supine hypotensive syndrome is relieved by placing the late-pregnant patient on her left side.
why: In late pregnancy, the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the woman lies supine, reducing blood return to the heart. Left lateral positioning moves the uterus off the vena cava and restores cardiac output.
wrong: The supine position is what compresses the vena cava; raising the legs does not relieve it.
Sitting upright does not reliably relieve caval compression and may worsen hypotension.
Prone positioning is impractical and unsafe in late pregnancy.

stem: A 2-year-old had a 1-minute generalized seizure at home. The child is now drowsy but breathing adequately, cries when touched, and feels hot. The mother says the child has had a fever since yesterday. What is the most appropriate care?
opts: Place the child in a cold bath to lower the fever quickly, then transport
Place the child on the side, give oxygen as needed, remove excess clothing, and transport
Give the child sips of cold water to help lower the temperature before transport
Reassure the mother that febrile seizures are harmless and transport is unnecessary
key: After a pediatric febrile seizure, protect the airway, cool passively, and transport for evaluation.
why: A postictal child is at risk of airway compromise, so positioning on the side with oxygen as needed comes first. Removing excess clothing allows passive cooling, and every seizure needs evaluation for causes such as meningitis.
wrong: Cold-water immersion can cause shivering and hypothermia and is not used for febrile seizures.
A drowsy postictal child should not be given anything by mouth because of aspiration risk.
A first seizure with fever needs medical evaluation to rule out serious causes such as meningitis.

stem: An 82-year-old woman tripped and struck her head on a table. She is alert and oriented, GCS 15, with a small forehead bruise and a mild headache. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Vital signs are normal. What is the best decision?
opts: Let her stay home, since her neurologic exam and vital signs are normal
Transport her, preferentially to a trauma center per the field triage guideline
Advise her to see her own physician tomorrow if the headache continues
Observe her on scene for 30 minutes before deciding on transport
key: Anticoagulant use and a ground-level fall with head strike in an older adult are 2021 field triage risk factors for transport.
why: In the 2021 field triage guideline, anticoagulant use and a low-level fall with significant head impact in an adult 65 or older are yellow (moderate-risk) criteria: preferential transport to a trauma center, which need not be the highest level. Anticoagulated patients can deteriorate hours after a head strike despite a normal first exam.
wrong: Anticoagulated older adults can deteriorate hours after a head strike despite a normal first exam.
Delaying evaluation risks missing a slowly expanding brain bleed.
Observation on scene delays imaging and does not rule out a bleed.

stem: A 6-year-old with a tracheostomy is in respiratory distress at home. You hear gurgling from the tube, RR 40, SpO2 86%. The parent says the tube often needs suctioning. What should you do first?
opts: Cover the stoma and ventilate by mouth and nose with a BVM
Suction the tracheostomy tube with sterile technique, limiting each pass
Remove the tracheostomy tube and wait for a replacement tube to arrive
Apply a nasal cannula at 4 L/min and transport the child with the parent
key: Distress with secretions in a tracheostomy tube is treated first by suctioning the tube.
why: Secretions are the most common cause of tracheostomy obstruction. Suctioning the tube with sterile technique and limited suction time restores the airway; ventilating through the mouth or changing the tube are steps if suctioning fails.
wrong: Ventilating through the mouth and nose is a later step if the tube cannot be cleared.
Removing the tube without a replacement in hand can lose the airway entirely.
A nasal cannula does not address the obstructed tube, which is how this child breathes.

stem: You are staffing the medical tent at a summer marathon. Classify each runner's presentation.
rows: Alert, dizzy, sweating heavily, nauseated, temperature 101°F
Collapsed and seizing, hot skin, temperature 105°F
Headache and muscle cramps, oriented, cool clammy skin
key: Altered mental status with a high core temperature means heat stroke; an intact mental status suggests heat exhaustion.
why: Heat stroke is defined by central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion, seizure, or collapse with a very high temperature; exertional heat stroke patients may still be sweating. Heat exhaustion patients remain oriented, with dizziness, nausea, cramps, and moist skin.

stem: A 70-year-old man was found in an unheated home in winter. He is confused, has stopped shivering, and his skin is cold. HR 48, RR 10. What is the most important handling consideration?
opts: Have him walk to the ambulance to generate body heat and avoid lifting him
Handle him gently and horizontally, remove wet clothing, and rewarm passively
Rub his arms and legs vigorously to restore circulation
Give him hot coffee to drink, then move him quickly to the warm ambulance
key: Severely hypothermic patients are handled gently and kept horizontal because rough movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation.
why: Confusion, loss of shivering, and bradycardia indicate severe hypothermia, and the cold heart is irritable. Gentle horizontal handling, removing wet clothing, and passive rewarming prevent further heat loss without provoking a dysrhythmia.
wrong: Exertion and rough movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation in a cold heart.
Vigorous rubbing damages tissue and can precipitate a dysrhythmia.
A confused patient should not drink, and caffeine does not rewarm.

stem: A lifeguard pulls a 7-year-old from a pool. The child is unresponsive, not breathing, and has no pulse. You and your partner have a BVM with oxygen and an AED. What is the best approach?
opts: Perform abdominal thrusts to drain water from the lungs first
Begin compression-only CPR and add ventilations after the AED arrives
Begin CPR at 15:2 with ventilations that produce visible chest rise
Delay CPR until the AED is attached and has analyzed the rhythm
key: Drowning arrest is hypoxic, so CPR must include effective ventilations; do not try to drain water.
why: Cardiac arrest after drowning results from hypoxia, so ventilation is essential. Two-rescuer child CPR uses 15:2 with breaths that make the chest rise, and the AED is attached as soon as it is ready without delaying CPR.
wrong: Abdominal thrusts do not remove water from the lungs and delay CPR.
Compression-only CPR does not address the hypoxia that caused the arrest.
CPR starts immediately; the AED is applied without delaying compressions.

stem: A 36-year-old hiker was bitten on the lower leg by a rattlesnake 15 minutes ago. The area is swollen and painful. He is alert with stable vital signs. What is the appropriate care?
opts: Apply a tourniquet tightly above the bite to keep the venom from spreading
Apply ice packs directly over the bite site to slow the spread of venom
Keep him calm, remove rings and tight items, splint the leg in neutral, and transport
Make a small incision over the bite and suction out as much venom as possible
key: Snakebite care: calm the patient, remove rings and tight items, immobilize the limb, and transport for antivenom.
why: Swelling spreads quickly, so jewelry and tight clothing are removed early. Limiting movement and transporting promptly to a facility with antivenom is the definitive approach.
wrong: Tourniquets concentrate venom locally and worsen tissue destruction.
Ice worsens local tissue damage.
Incision and suction do not remove meaningful venom and add bleeding, tissue damage, and infection.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has sudden facial droop, arm drift, and garbled speech, with a positive stroke scale. She was last known well 50 minutes ago. A community hospital is 8 minutes away; a stroke center is 18 minutes away. Your destination protocol directs suspected stroke to stroke centers within that transport time. What should you do?
opts: Transport to the closer community hospital because it is 10 minutes faster
Transport to the stroke center and pre-notify them with her last-known-well time
Remain on scene for several minutes to see whether her symptoms resolve
Request air medical transport and wait on scene for the helicopter
key: Suspected stroke goes to the stroke-capable destination per protocol, with early notification and the last-known-well time.
why: Stroke centers can provide time-sensitive treatments such as thrombolysis and clot retrieval. Following the destination protocol and pre-notifying with the last-known-well time lets the team be ready on arrival.
wrong: Protocol directs her to a stroke center; a hospital that cannot provide definitive care may delay treatment.
Waiting on scene wastes the time-limited treatment window.
An 18-minute ground transport is faster than waiting for and loading an aircraft.

stem: You are triaging adults at a highway crash. Under the 2021 National Guideline for the Field Triage of Injured Patients, which findings are high-risk (red) criteria that direct transport to the highest-level trauma center available? Select THREE.
opts: A tourniquet was needed to control extremity bleeding
Unable to follow commands (motor GCS less than 6)
Suspected pelvic fracture
Isolated closed wrist deformity with normal vital signs
Ground-level fall in a 30-year-old with knee abrasions
Airbag deployed; alert, normal vital signs, and no complaints
key: 2021 red criteria include bleeding needing a tourniquet or packing, inability to follow commands, and suspected pelvic fracture.
why: The 2021 guideline groups injury patterns and mental status or vital sign findings as red criteria for the highest-level trauma center. Active bleeding requiring a tourniquet, motor GCS below 6, and suspected pelvic fracture are all on that list.
wrong: An isolated distal extremity injury with normal vitals does not meet red criteria.
A low-energy fall in a young adult with minor injuries does not meet high-risk criteria.
Airbag deployment alone in an uninjured patient with normal findings is not a red criterion.

stem: A 66-year-old man has vomited blood twice and is now pale and cool. He is alert, RR 22, HR 124, BP 84/52, with no trauma or breathing difficulty. How should you position him for transport?
opts: Supine and kept warm, ready to turn him if he vomits
Seated upright at 90 degrees on the stretcher
Supine with the stretcher tilted steeply head-down
Prone with his face turned to one side
key: A patient in shock without breathing difficulty is transported supine and kept warm.
why: Supine positioning supports blood flow to the brain in shock, and preventing heat loss limits worsening coagulopathy. Because he is vomiting blood, the EMT keeps suction ready and is prepared to turn him.
wrong: Upright positioning can worsen hypotension and brain perfusion in shock.
Steep head-down positioning impairs breathing, raises aspiration risk, and is no longer recommended.
Prone positioning hides the airway and restricts breathing.

stem: You are calling the receiving hospital about a 59-year-old man with chest pain. Which radio report is most appropriate?
opts: Medic 4, 10 minutes out: 59-year-old male, chest pain 30 minutes, cardiac history, BP 150/90, HR 96, SpO2 97%, aspirin given
Medic 4, inbound with chest pain; will give the patient's full name, home address, and insurance information next
Medic 4, we've got a guy having a heart attack, coming in hot, see you soon
Medic 4, 10 minutes out with a stable patient; details will follow when we arrive
key: A radio report gives unit, ETA, age and sex, chief complaint, pertinent history, vital signs, and treatment given.
why: The hospital needs enough concise clinical information to prepare: who is coming, when, what is wrong, how stable the patient is, and what has been done. Identifying details are left for the in-person handoff.
wrong: Names, addresses, and insurance are not needed by radio and raise privacy concerns.
It lacks vital signs and treatment and uses slang and an unconfirmed diagnosis.
It gives the hospital nothing to prepare with.

stem: You arrive at the emergency department with a patient whose condition changed after your radio report: her BP dropped from 124/80 to 96/60 after nitroglycerin. The triage nurse is busy with another patient. What is the correct handoff action?
opts: Leave her on a hallway bed with your written report and return to service
Give a verbal report, including the BP change, to the nurse or physician who assumes care
Tell the registration clerk about the BP change and leave your written report
Finish your written report first, then give it to whoever is available
key: Care is transferred only by verbal report to a qualified provider who assumes care, including changes since the radio report.
why: Leaving a patient without handing off to an equal or higher level provider can be abandonment. The verbal report must highlight changes such as the drop in BP after nitroglycerin, with the written report to follow.
wrong: Leaving without transferring care to a qualified provider can constitute abandonment.
A registration clerk cannot assume clinical care.
An important change should be reported verbally now; documentation follows.

stem: Your two-EMT crew is 40 minutes from the nearest hospital with a 70-year-old man who has fever, chills, new confusion, HR 124, RR 28, and BP 78/46. An ALS unit is available to meet you along the route. What is the best decision?
opts: Begin transport and request an ALS rendezvous en route
Stay at the residence until the ALS unit arrives there
Transport without ALS because sepsis needs only hospital antibiotics
Request air medical and wait on scene until it lands
key: For a long transport with an unstable patient, start moving and arrange an ALS intercept rather than waiting on scene.
why: Suspected septic shock with a long transport benefits from ALS interventions such as IV fluids. A rendezvous brings ALS to the patient without losing time, while waiting on scene for any resource delays definitive care.
wrong: Waiting on scene adds time; a rendezvous lets ALS reach him without stopping progress toward the hospital.
Septic shock needs IV fluids and ALS assessment; a long transport makes ALS valuable.
Waiting on scene for an aircraft delays care when a ground ALS intercept is readily available.
